Recursion.explanation: Recursion is a programming technique in which a method calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. A recursive solution must have a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that moves the problem toward the base case.
learning_path: Solve array and string recursion problems

What is Recursion.explanation: Recursion occurs when a method calls itself directly or indirectly. Each call works on a smaller or simpler version of the original problem.
points_to_remember: A recursive method calls itself.
Every recursion needs a stopping condition.
The stopping condition is called the base case.
The recursive call should move toward the base case.

Base Case.explanation: The base case is the condition that stops further recursive calls. Without a correct base case, recursion may continue indefinitely and eventually cause StackOverflowError in Java.
points_to_remember: Every recursive algorithm needs one or more stopping conditions.
The base case should return a known result.
The recursive case must eventually reach the base case.

Recursive Case.explanation: The recursive case is the part of the method that calls itself with a smaller, simpler, or modified input.

Call Stack.explanation: Every recursive method call creates a new stack frame containing local variables, parameters, and return information. The frames remain on the stack until the base case is reached and calls begin returning.
Call Stack.example: print(3) first creates calls for 3, 2, and 1. After reaching 0, the calls return in reverse order.
points_to_remember: Recursive calls are stored on the call stack.
The deepest call executes before earlier calls continue.
Large recursion depth can cause StackOverflowError.

Tracing Recursion.explanation: Tracing recursion means manually following every recursive call and return. This is one of the most important skills for understanding recursive algorithms.
Tracing Recursion.practice_tip: When tracing recursion, separate the downward calls from the upward returns.

Indirect Recursion.explanation: A method calls another method, which eventually calls the original method.
points_to_remember: The recursion can involve multiple methods.
At least one path must eventually reach a stopping condition.

Tail Recursion.explanation: A recursive call is tail-recursive when it is the final operation performed by the method.
Tail Recursion.important_note: Java does not generally perform tail-call optimization, so tail recursion can still consume stack space.

Head Recursion.explanation: In head recursion, the recursive call happens before the main processing of the current call.

Tree Recursion.explanation: Tree recursion occurs when a recursive method makes more than one recursive call, creating a tree-shaped call structure.
points_to_remember: Tree recursion can generate many repeated calls.
Naive Fibonacci recursion has exponential time complexity.
Memoization can remove repeated calculations.

Nested Recursion.explanation: Nested recursion occurs when the argument of a recursive call itself contains another recursive call.
points_to_remember: Nested recursion can be difficult to trace.
The inner recursive call must complete before the outer call proceeds.

Factorial.explanation: The factorial of n is n * (n-1) * ... * 1. By definition, 0! = 1.

Sum of First N Numbers.explanation: Recursion can calculate the sum of integers from 1 to n.

Power.explanation: Calculate x raised to the power n recursively.

Fast Power.explanation: Exponentiation by squaring reduces the number of recursive calls by dividing the exponent approximately in half at each step.
points_to_remember: Divide the exponent by 2.
This is much faster than multiplying x n times.

Fibonacci.explanation: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1.
Fibonacci.warning: Naive recursive Fibonacci repeatedly solves the same subproblems and is inefficient for large n.

GCD.explanation: Euclid's algorithm calculates the greatest common divisor recursively.
GCD.formula: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)

Decimal To Binary.explanation: A decimal number can be converted to binary recursively by processing the quotient and then printing the remainder.
points_to_remember: The recursive call processes the higher-order bits first.
The remainder gives the current binary digit.

Sum Of Array.explanation: Recursively calculate the sum of all elements in an array.

Maximum Element.explanation: Recursively find the maximum element of an array.

Linear Search.explanation: Recursively search for a target value in an array.

Binary Search.explanation: Recursive binary search repeatedly divides a sorted array into two halves.

Check Sorted Array.explanation: Recursively determine whether an array is sorted in non-decreasing order.

Reverse Array.explanation: Recursively reverse an array using two pointers.

Reverse String.explanation: A string can be reversed recursively by taking the last character and recursively processing the remaining string.
Reverse String.complexity_note: Using substring and repeated string concatenation can cause additional overhead in Java. For production code, a character array or StringBuilder may be preferable.

Palindrome Check.explanation: A string is a palindrome if it reads the same from both directions. Recursion can compare characters at both ends.

Remove Character.explanation: Recursively create a string while skipping a specified character.

complexity.time: O(n^2) in the worst case due to immutable String concatenation

Count Character.explanation: Recursively count how many times a character occurs in a string.

Tower of Hanoi.explanation: Tower of Hanoi moves n disks from a source peg to a destination peg using an auxiliary peg. A disk can only be placed on a larger disk.

Josephus Problem.explanation: The Josephus problem asks for the survivor when people arranged in a circle are eliminated at a fixed interval. It has a useful recursive formulation.

divide_and_conquer.explanation: Divide and conquer recursively divides a problem into smaller subproblems, solves them, and combines their results.

pattern: Divide the search range into two parts.

Merge Sort.explanation: Merge sort recursively divides an array into halves, sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves.

Quick Sort.explanation: Quick sort recursively partitions an array around a pivot and sorts the resulting partitions.

complexity.space: O(log n) average recursion depth; O(n) worst case

Reverse Linked List.explanation: A linked list can be reversed recursively by reversing the remainder of the list and then attaching the current node after the next node.

Find Length.explanation: Recursively count nodes in a linked list.

Tree Traversal - Preorder.explanation: Preorder visits root, left subtree, and right subtree.

Tree Traversal - Inorder.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree, root, and right subtree.
Tree Traversal - Inorder.important_note: Inorder traversal of a binary search tree produces values in sorted order.

Tree Traversal - Postorder.explanation: Postorder visits the left subtree, right subtree, and root.

Tree Height.explanation: The height of a binary tree can be calculated recursively by finding the larger height of the two subtrees.

complexity.space: O(h), where h is tree height

Count Nodes.explanation: Recursively count nodes in a binary tree.

backtracking.explanation: Backtracking is a recursive technique that builds a solution step by step. When a choice leads to an invalid or unwanted state, the algorithm undoes the choice and tries another option.

Generate Subsets.explanation: Every element has two choices: include it or exclude it. Recursion explores both choices.

Generate Subsequences.explanation: A subsequence is created by maintaining relative order while choosing whether to include each character.

complexity.time: O(2^n) outputs, with Java String construction adding overhead

Permutations.explanation: Permutations generate every possible ordering of elements. Backtracking swaps or chooses elements while recursively constructing the permutation.

Combination Sum.explanation: Backtracking can find combinations of numbers that satisfy a target sum.
points_to_remember: Backtracking changes state before recursion.
The state must be restored after recursion.
Incorrect undo operations can produce incorrect results.

N Queens.explanation: The N-Queens problem places N queens on an N×N chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Backtracking tries possible positions row by row.
pattern: Check whether the position is safe.
Remove the queen if the choice fails.

Maze Backtracking.explanation: A maze can be solved recursively by moving to valid neighboring cells and backtracking when a path does not lead to the destination.
points_to_remember: Mark visited cells.
Try possible directions.
Backtrack when no direction works.

dynamic_programming_connection.explanation: Many recursive problems contain overlapping subproblems. Dynamic programming improves these solutions by storing previously computed results.
dynamic_programming_connection.important_concept: Before converting recursion to dynamic programming, identify repeated subproblems and define the state.

advantages: Natural for tree and graph structures.
disadvantages: Function-call overhead can matter in performance-sensitive code.

advantages: Often easier to optimize for simple loops.
disadvantages: Some problems are less natural to express iteratively.
Backtracking and tree algorithms may require explicit stacks and additional state.

problem_solving_template.step_1: Identify whether the problem can be reduced to a smaller version of itself.
problem_solving_template.step_4: Determine how the current problem depends on a smaller problem.
problem_solving_template.step_6: Ensure every recursive call moves toward the base case.
problem_solving_template.step_7: Trace the recursion with a small input.
problem_solving_template.step_9: Check whether repeated subproblems suggest memoization.
problem_solving_template.step_10: If choices are being explored, consider backtracking.

important_patterns.example: optimized Fibonacci and other overlapping-subproblem problems

common_mistakes: Writing a base case that can never be reached.
Not changing the input in the recursive call.
Using recursion when iteration would be significantly simpler.
Forgetting to return the recursive result.
Confusing the order of operations before and after the recursive call.
Not understanding how values return through the call stack.
Using naive recursion for problems with overlapping subproblems.
Forgetting to undo state during backtracking.
Ignoring recursion depth for large inputs.
Using string concatenation heavily inside recursive loops.

beginner: Print numbers from 1 to N using head recursion.
Print numbers from N to 1 using tail recursion.
Find the sum of the first N numbers.
Count the digits of a number.
array_and_string: Find the maximum element in an array.
Find the minimum element in an array.
Calculate the sum of an array.
Check whether an array is sorted.
Check whether a string is a palindrome.
Remove a character from a string.

final_summary: Recursion means solving a problem by calling the same method on a smaller problem.
Every recursive algorithm needs a base case.
The recursive case must move toward the base case.
The Java call stack stores active recursive calls.
BFS, DFS, tree traversal, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking all use recursive ideas in different ways.
Memoization can optimize recursion when subproblems overlap.
Backtracking follows the choose, explore, and undo pattern.
Always analyze both time complexity and recursion-stack space.
Practice tracing recursive calls before attempting advanced recursive problems.
For Java, be aware that very deep recursion can cause StackOverflowError.
